description: We're a small team from Riyadh working on the Flame in Freefall challenge. We'll use NASA's microgravity combustion data from the ISS to train a simple AI model that predicts how fire behaves in space, and turn it into fire safety insights for astronauts. We're into math, Python and AI. We're looking for 1-2 teammates with skills in data analysis, machine learning, data visualization or slide design. If you like space and data, join us!
summary:
Project Zero-G Ignition is an interactive dashboard that helps mission designers find the NASA fire experiments that matter most for their mission. We collected 31 combustion experiment records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository and NASA Glenn’s combustion science pages, including BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE and FM2. For each one we recorded the fuel type, oxygen level, pressure, airflow, what was measured, and whether it is about fire prevention, detection or suppression.

The user picks a mission (Spacecraft, Moon Base or Rover) and the dashboard ranks every experiment with a transparent 100-point score based on atmosphere, safety area, fuel type and gravity. Each result has a plain-English summary and a fire safety insight, written with AI assistance and checked by our team. A chart of oxygen against pressure shows which experiments are close to Moon conditions.

This matters because future Moon habitats will use oxygen-rich, low-pressure air, where materials burn more easily, and very few experiments have tested those conditions.
details:
What it does
Project Zero-G Ignition is a web dashboard that ranks NASA’s space fire experiments by how relevant they are to a chosen mission. The user picks Spacecraft, Moon Base or Rover. The dashboard then scores 31 experiment records out of 100 and shows, for each one, a plain-English summary and a fire safety insight.

How it works
We built a table of NASA combustion experiments (BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE, FM2 and others) with fuel type, oxygen level, pressure, airflow, what was measured, and whether the work is about prevention, detection or suppression. Each mission has its own atmosphere, gravity and priorities. The score has four parts: atmosphere match (40 points), safety area (25), fuel type (20) and gravity (15). A chart of oxygen against pressure marks Earth, the Moon base and a spacesuit, so you can see at a glance which experiments are close to Moon conditions.

Benefits and impact
Future Moon habitats and rovers are planned to use air with 34% oxygen at 8.2 psi, where materials burn more easily than in Earth air. NASA’s experiment results are spread across many pages and reports. Our tool puts them in one place and points engineers, students and mission planners to the most useful evidence first. It also shows the gaps: most experiments ran in Earth-like air, and only one is built for lunar gravity.

Tools
Python, Streamlit, pandas and Plotly, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud. The data is a CSV file that anyone can open and edit.

Use of AI
We used Claude (Anthropic) to help collect experiment details from NASA sources, write the summaries and insights, write the app code and draft the slides. Our team reviewed the content.

What makes it creative
Instead of a plain list, the same data re-ranks itself for each mission, and the formula is simple enough for anyone to check. Experiments with missing data are labelled as such and not plotted.

What we considered
We kept the scoring transparent, wrote every summary in plain English, and marked where each oxygen and pressure value comes from: published, assumed cabin air, or not given in NASA’s summary.
